title: Clinical Reasoning
summary: How clinicians turn a complaint into a diagnosis and a disposition: illness scripts and the biases that break them, the history and physical, the differential, what a test actually proves, the decision rules, the note, and the handoff.

lessons.title: How clinicians actually think
lessons.body:
## The expert does not run a checklist

Watch an experienced provider walk into a room. In four seconds, before a single question, they have already sorted the patient into sick or not sick and pulled up two or three diseases worth thinking about. They are not being sloppy. They are matching what they see against thousands of stored patterns.

Psychologists call that fast, automatic matching **System 1**. The slow, deliberate, one-fact-at-a-time kind of thinking is **System 2** (analytic reasoning). Every clinician runs both. The skill is knowing which one you are in.

## Illness scripts are the patterns

The stored pattern has a name: an **illness script**. A script has three parts.

1. **Who gets it** (epidemiology and risk factors). "A 55-year-old smoker with diabetes and high blood pressure."
2. **What it does to the body and how fast** (mechanism and time course). "A plaque ruptures, a coronary artery clots, pain builds over minutes and then stays."
3. **What it looks like** (key features, including the findings that should be there and the ones that should not). "Pressure, brought on by exertion, radiates to jaw or left arm, with sweating and nausea. Not sharp, not reproduced by pressing on the chest."

A first-year student carries textbook lists. A clinician carries scripts. You build scripts by seeing patients and then reading about the disease the same day, while the face is still in your head.

> **Key:** A differential diagnosis is a competition between illness scripts. The more complete your scripts, the faster and safer the match.

## Where each system fails

System 1 fails on the atypical presentation: the diabetic woman whose heart attack shows up only as nausea and fatigue, the 82-year-old whose pneumonia shows up as confusion and a fall. It also fails when you are tired, rushed, interrupted, or emotionally loaded about the patient.

System 2 fails differently. It is slow, it burns attention, and nobody can run it on every patient in a department with 40 people waiting. Used on everything, it turns into indecision and a shotgun workup.

The working rule: **pattern-match first, then deliberately verify.** Let the fast system generate candidates, then spend 30 seconds of slow thinking making sure the dangerous alternatives do not fit.

## Sick or not sick

Before any diagnosis there is a cruder and more important judgment: is this patient about to get worse? That judgment is the **gestalt**, and it is built from things you can name out loud.

- **The doorway impression.** Color, work of breathing, posture, whether they look at you when you come in, whether they can finish a sentence. A patient sitting bolt upright leaning on their hands (tripoding) is in trouble before anyone speaks.
- **The vitals trend, not the single set.** A heart rate that goes `96`, then `108`, then `124` over an hour is a story. One reading is a snapshot.
- **The mismatch.** Pain far out of proportion to the exam. Normal-looking numbers on a terrible-looking patient. A blood pressure of `118/70` that looks fine until you learn this patient lives at `170/95`.

> **On shift:** "Something is wrong with this guy" is data, not a mood. Experienced staff are reading skin, respiratory rate, and posture in seconds. When you get that feeling, say it out loud to a nurse or provider, and say what triggered it.

## Building the gestalt on purpose

Gestalt is pattern recognition, so it grows the same way: repetitions plus feedback. Two habits do most of the work.

Keep a **case log**. After a shift, write five lines on each interesting patient, with no names, no dates of birth, no identifiers: chief complaint, what was ordered, what it showed, where the patient went, one thing learned. Fifty entries is a real education, and cases you can discuss in specifics are also what turns a PA school interview answer from generic into concrete.

Ask one question per shift: **"What are you worried about with this patient?"** You are not asking for the diagnosis. You are asking which dangerous thing the provider is ruling out, and that is where the reasoning actually lives.
keyPoints: Fast pattern recognition (System 1) and slow analytic reasoning (System 2) both run; the skill is knowing which one you are in.
An illness script is who gets it, what it does and how fast, and what it looks like.
Pattern-match first, then deliberately verify that the dangerous alternatives do not fit.
Sick or not sick comes from the doorway impression, the vitals trend, and mismatches, and it is worth saying out loud.
Build judgment deliberately with a de-identified case log and by asking what the provider is worried about.

checks.q: A provider glances at a patient from the doorway and immediately says, get a 12-lead and a line. What kind of reasoning is that, and what is its main weakness?
choices: System 1 pattern recognition; it fails on atypical presentations
System 2 analytic reasoning; it fails because it is too slow to use
System 1 pattern recognition; it fails because it ignores vital signs
System 2 analytic reasoning; it fails only in elderly patients
checks.why: Instant recognition from a glance is System 1 pattern matching. Its weakness is the presentation that does not match the stored script, such as the diabetic or elderly patient with a silent heart attack. System 2 is the slow, deliberate mode, safe but too expensive to run on everyone.

checks.q: Which description best captures an illness script?
choices: A list of every disease that can cause a given symptom
The fixed order in which a physical exam is performed
Who gets the disease, what it does to the body and how fast, and what it looks like
The sensitivity and specificity of the tests used to diagnose it
checks.why: A script bundles epidemiology and risk, mechanism and time course, and the key positive and negative features. A bare list of causes is a differential, not a script, and test characteristics only matter after a script has generated a candidate.

checks.q: Serial rechecks show a heart rate of 96, then 108, then 124, while the blood pressure holds at 122/78. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
choices: Normal variation, since only the blood pressure matters
A rising trend consistent with early compensation, which should be reported
Monitor artifact, which is common at higher rates
Nothing to report until the systolic pressure drops below 90
checks.why: Trends beat snapshots. A climbing heart rate with a still-normal pressure is what early compensated shock looks like, because the body defends pressure by speeding the heart. By the time the systolic falls, compensation has already failed, which is exactly the delay that trend-watching exists to prevent.

lessons.title: The biases that hurt patients, and the habits that stop them
lessons.body:
## A bias is a shortcut that misfired

Diagnostic error is usually not caused by not knowing the disease. Reviews of missed diagnoses keep finding the same thing: the clinician knew the disease existed and did not think of it, or thought of it and dropped it too early. The shortcuts that make you fast are the same ones that make you wrong.

Five show up constantly in an emergency department.

### Anchoring

You fix on the first piece of information, and everything afterward gets read through it.

Example: triage writes "anxiety attack." The patient is 34, panting, tingling in both hands. Everyone treats anxiety. Nobody asks about the flight from Los Angeles last night or the calf that has been sore for three days. It is a pulmonary embolism, a clot in the lung.

### Premature closure

You stop looking once you have an answer that fits. It is anchoring's finisher.

Example: flank pain with blood in the urine in a patient with known kidney stones, so it is a stone. The scan that nobody ordered would have shown a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm, which produces flank pain and blood in the urine in a 68-year-old smoker.

### Availability

Whatever you have seen most recently or most vividly feels most likely.

Example: you helped with two septic pneumonias this week, so the next febrile cougher gets the same workup and nobody looks at the leg with the spreading red margin. Availability also runs backward: you have never personally seen an aortic dissection, so it does not occur to you.

### Diagnosis momentum

A label picked up early hardens into fact as it is handed along, from family to EMS to triage to the tech to the provider to the consultant, with nobody re-examining the original evidence.

Example: "seizure" from a frightened spouse becomes "seizure" on the run sheet, becomes "post-ictal" at triage, becomes a neurology consult. The rhythm strip later shows the episode was a run of ventricular tachycardia.

### The frequent flyer bias

Also called attribution bias: the patient's identity or history explains the complaint away. It gets applied to people with substance use disorder, psychiatric diagnoses, homelessness, chronic pain, or a thick chart of prior visits.

Example: a man who comes in intoxicated twice a month arrives "drunk again" and gets a hallway bed to sleep it off. The head strike he took four hours ago has become a subdural hematoma. These patients carry more disease than average, not less, which is part of why they keep coming back.

> **Trap:** The bias is not being rude to the patient. It is quietly lowering your threshold of evidence for the boring explanation because you already decided who this person is.

## Three habits that actually work

**The diagnostic time-out.** Before you commit, before the disposition, before the handoff, stop for 20 seconds and answer three questions: what is my working diagnosis, what does not fit, and what is the worst thing this could be.

**"What else could this be?"** Say it out loud and force at least two alternatives. Forcing alternatives is the debiasing technique that most consistently beats simply trying harder or being told to be careful.

**Worst-first.** The emergency mindset is not "what does this patient probably have." It is "what could kill this patient in the next few hours, and have I excluded it?" Chest pain gets acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, and esophageal rupture considered before anyone says reflux. You name the likely diagnosis after the killers are cleared, not instead of clearing them.

> **Key:** Ruling out is a verb with evidence attached. "Pulmonary embolism considered and excluded by PERC" is reasoning. "Probably not a PE" is a hope.
keyPoints: Most diagnostic error is a thinking failure, not a knowledge failure.
Anchoring fixes you on the first fact; premature closure stops the search as soon as something fits.
Availability overweights what you saw recently; diagnosis momentum lets an early label harden as it is handed along.
Attribution or frequent-flyer bias lowers the evidence threshold for patients with thick charts, who carry more disease, not less.
Debias with a 20-second diagnostic time-out, forcing two alternatives, and ruling out killers before naming the likely diagnosis.

checks.q: A 61-year-old woman with epigastric burning is labeled likely gastritis at triage, treated with antacids, and nearly discharged before an ECG shows an inferior STEMI. Which pair of biases best describes what happened?
choices: Anchoring and premature closure
Availability and outcome bias
Attribution bias and the sunk cost fallacy
Base-rate neglect and hindsight bias
checks.why: The first label set the frame, which is anchoring, and the search stopped once an explanation seemed to fit, which is premature closure. Availability is over-weighting what you have seen recently, attribution bias explains a complaint away by who the patient is, and outcome and hindsight biases only operate after the result is known.

checks.q: Which single question is the strongest bedside debiasing tool?
choices: Have I seen a case like this before?
What else could this be?
What is the most common cause of this symptom?
Does the patient agree with my diagnosis?
checks.why: Forcing alternatives is the technique that most reliably reduces diagnostic error. Asking whether you have seen it before recruits availability, and reaching for the most common cause reinforces the very pattern you are trying to test. Patient agreement is not a check on accuracy.

checks.q: What does the worst-first mindset require before a clinician names the likely diagnosis?
choices: A complete review of systems on every patient
Consultant agreement with the working diagnosis
That the dangerous causes have been actively considered and excluded with stated evidence
That every available laboratory test has resulted
checks.why: Worst-first means the killers are addressed first with evidence attached, such as a decision rule or a test, and the likely diagnosis is named afterward. A full review of systems, consultant agreement, and a complete lab panel are none of them the same as actively excluding a specific dangerous disease.

lessons.title: The history and physical, start to finish
lessons.body:
## The history makes the diagnosis

Studies in general medical clinics have found the history alone points to the correct diagnosis in roughly 70 to 80 percent of cases, with the exam and the tests mostly confirming it. The history is the highest-yield test in medicine and it is free.

It has a fixed order, and the order is the same everywhere so that anyone can find any piece of it in three seconds.

## Chief complaint

One line, in the patient's own words, with a duration. "Chest pressure for 2 hours." Not "rule out MI," which is your hypothesis, not their complaint. Quoting preserves information, because "my chest is tight" and "my chest is ripping" point to different diseases.

## History of present illness

Two mnemonics, same job. **OPQRST** is built for pain:

- **O**nset: what they were doing when it started, sudden or gradual
- **P**rovocation and palliation: what makes it worse, what makes it better
- **Q**uality: the patient's own adjective, such as pressure, sharp, burning, tearing
- **R**adiation: where else it goes
- **S**everity: `0` to `10`, now and at its worst
- **T**iming: constant or in waves, how long, ever had it before

**OLDCARTS** covers non-pain complaints: Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating and Alleviating factors, Radiation, Timing, Severity.

Then the part beginners skip: **pertinent positives and negatives**. These are the symptoms you asked about because of your differential, recorded whether present or absent. For chest pain: "Positive for sweating and nausea. Denies fever, cough, leg swelling, or tearing pain to the back."

> **Key:** A pertinent negative is proof you thought about a disease. A note with no negatives reads like a note with no differential.

## The rest of the history

- **Past medical history.** Diagnoses with dates and severity. "Diabetes" is weak. "Type 2 diabetes since 2014, on insulin, last A1c `9.1`" is useful.
- **Past surgical history.** What and when. Prior abdominal surgery makes bowel obstruction from adhesions live. Prior bypass or stents changes chest pain pretest probability immediately.
- **Medications.** Name, dose, and whether they are actually taking them. Blood thinners, beta blockers (which blunt the tachycardia you rely on), steroids, insulin, and immunosuppressants all change the workup.
- **Allergies with the reaction.** "Penicillin, hives" and "penicillin, upset stomach" are different facts. One is an allergy, one is a side effect.
- **Family history,** only what matters here: first-degree relatives with early heart disease (men under 55, women under 65), sudden death, aneurysm, clotting disorders, certain cancers.
- **Social history.** Tobacco in pack-years, alcohol in drinks per day or week, drugs including route, occupation and exposures, who they live with and whether they can manage stairs, and sexual history when the complaint makes it relevant. Living situation is not small talk. It decides disposition.
- **Review of systems.** A quick sweep of the systems you have not already covered, hunting for a symptom the patient never thought to mention. A full review is 10 or more systems; a focused one is the 2 to 4 that touch your differential.

## The physical exam, in the order it is done

Head to toe, so nothing gets dropped.

1. **General appearance and vital signs:** distress, color, work of breathing
2. **Head, eyes, ears, nose, throat:** pupils, mucous membranes, airway
3. **Neck:** jugular venous distention, trachea midline, stiffness, lymph nodes
4. **Lungs:** inspect the chest, then listen in all fields front and back
5. **Cardiovascular:** rate, rhythm, murmurs, peripheral pulses, swelling
6. **Abdomen:** inspect, listen before you press, then percuss and palpate, tender area last
7. **Extremities:** pulses, swelling, calf tenderness, range of motion
8. **Skin:** rashes, wounds, temperature, capillary refill
9. **Neurologic:** mental status, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, coordination, gait
10. **Back:** midline tenderness, flank tenderness

## Focused versus full

An emergency history and physical is **hypothesis-driven**: chief complaint, focused history of present illness, the past history that changes management now, the few systems that matter, and the exam that confirms or excludes the killers. It can be done well in 6 minutes.

A full admission history and physical is **complete**: full review of systems, full past history, full exam, because the admitting team owns the whole patient for days.

> **On shift:** These are two real documents, not thorough versus lazy. The emergency note answers whether this person needs something in the next hour and where they go. The admission note answers who this person is and what the plan is for the next three days.
keyPoints: The history alone points to the diagnosis in roughly 70 to 80 percent of cases.
Chief complaint is one line in the patient's words with a duration, never a hypothesis.
OPQRST for pain, OLDCARTS for everything else, plus pertinent positives and negatives driven by your differential.
Record allergies with the reaction, and medications with whether they are actually being taken.
The emergency H and P is hypothesis-driven and focused; the admission H and P is complete because that team owns the patient for days.

checks.q: Which chief complaint is written correctly?
choices: Rule out acute coronary syndrome
Abdominal pain, possible appendicitis
My chest feels like something is sitting on it, for 3 hours
Patient is a poor historian
checks.why: The complaint is the patient's own words plus a duration, and the adjective carries diagnostic weight. The first two are hypotheses rather than complaints, and labeling someone a poor historian records a judgment instead of information.

checks.q: Why is the abdomen auscultated before it is palpated?
choices: Because pressing first alters bowel sounds and makes the patient guard against the rest of the exam
Because bowel sounds are the most reliable finding in abdominal pain
Because percussion is painful and should always come last
Because the stethoscope must be warmed before contact
checks.why: Listening first preserves unaltered bowel sounds, and saving palpation for last, with the tender area last of all, keeps the rest of the exam usable. Bowel sounds are in fact one of the weaker findings, which is exactly why you should not destroy them for nothing.

checks.q: A patient reports that penicillin gives him an upset stomach. How should this be recorded and interpreted?
choices: As anaphylaxis, since all penicillin reactions are treated the same way
As a side effect, documented with the reaction, which does not by itself rule out the drug class
As a true allergy requiring avoidance of every beta-lactam antibiotic
It does not need to be documented at all
checks.why: Gastrointestinal upset is a predictable side effect, not an immune reaction; hives, swelling, or trouble breathing would be an allergy. Recording the reaction rather than only the word is what keeps a whole antibiotic class available, and it still belongs in the chart.

lessons.title: Building a differential
lessons.body:
## A differential is a ranked list, not a brainstorm

The **differential diagnosis** is the set of diseases that could explain this presentation, ordered so that the order drives what happens next. Three rankings run at the same time.

- **Must not miss.** Kills or maims if missed, so it gets excluded first even at low probability.
- **Most likely.** Highest probability given who this patient is.
- **Most treatable.** Where finding it changes management right now. A pulmonary embolism you can anticoagulate outranks a viral syndrome you cannot touch.

A good plan handles all three: exclude the killers, treat the likely, and do not spend a workup on a diagnosis whose discovery changes nothing.

## Building it from the complaint

Start from the complaint, not from the chart. Two methods, both mechanical on purpose, because mechanical beats memory when you are tired.

**Anatomy from the outside in.** For a body region, walk the layers and then the organs inside the box. Right upper quadrant pain: skin and abdominal wall, ribs and muscle, pleura and the base of the right lung, liver, gallbladder and bile ducts, duodenum, head of the pancreas, right kidney, hepatic flexure of the colon. Nine structures, nine candidate diseases, none of them recalled from a list.

**VINDICATE** for a systemic or confusing presentation. It is a category checklist you run when anatomy gives you nothing.

| Letter | Category | Example in altered mental status |
|---|---|---|
| V | Vascular | stroke, intracranial hemorrhage |
| I | Infectious | meningitis, sepsis, urinary infection in the elderly |
| N | Neoplastic | brain mass with swelling |
| D | Degenerative and Drugs | dementia, opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol withdrawal |
| I | Iatrogenic and Idiopathic | a new medication, a dosing error |
| C | Congenital | inherited metabolic disease |
| A | Autoimmune | lupus affecting the brain, thyroid disease |
| T | Trauma and Toxins | subdural hematoma, carbon monoxide |
| E | Endocrine and Metabolic | low blood sugar, sodium derangement, thyroid storm |

At this stage you are generating, not deciding. Recognition level is enough. You need to know these categories exist, not to be able to work each one up.

## Narrowing it

Now the history and exam earn their keep. Every question and every maneuver should move at least one diagnosis up or down.

A headache that was maximal within seconds pushes subarachnoid hemorrhage up. A normal temperature pushes meningitis down but does not exclude it in an elderly or immunosuppressed patient. Chest pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall nudges a musculoskeletal cause up, but it does not exclude acute coronary syndrome, because roughly `7%` of patients with reproducible chest wall tenderness turn out to be having a coronary event anyway.

> **Trap:** Nothing you find at the bedside rules out a killer by itself. Individual findings shift probability. Decision rules and tests are what exclude.

## The three-item habit

Carrying twenty possibilities is the same as carrying none. The habit experienced clinicians actually use, and the one that makes you sound like you belong, is to name three.

"For this chest pain I am thinking acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and pneumonia. Coronary because of the risk factors and the exertional pattern, embolism because of the flight last week, pneumonia because of the fever and cough. Dissection is least likely, but I would want pressures in both arms."

Three named diagnoses, one reason each, one honest outlier with the thing you would check. It is short enough to say in a hallway and complete enough to act on.

> **Key:** If your differential does not change what you do next, it is not a differential, it is a list.
keyPoints: A differential is ranked three ways at once: must not miss, most likely, most treatable.
Generate candidates mechanically, by anatomy from the outside in or by the VINDICATE categories.
Every history question and exam maneuver should move at least one diagnosis up or down.
Bedside findings shift probability; rules and tests are what exclude a killer.
Say three diagnoses with one reason each plus one honest outlier and the thing you would check.

checks.q: Why are must-not-miss diagnoses addressed before the most likely diagnosis?
choices: They are more common in an emergency department than benign causes
The cost of missing them is severe and irreversible, so they are excluded even at low probability
They are usually easier and faster to exclude than common conditions
Reimbursement rules require imaging for them first
checks.why: The ranking is driven by consequence, not frequency. Killers are generally less common and often harder, not easier, to exclude, and the likely diagnosis gets named after the dangerous ones are addressed.

checks.q: A 70-year-old arrives confused with no obvious source. Using VINDICATE, which grouping correctly matches a category to a cause?
choices: Vascular: benzodiazepine overdose
Neoplastic: alcohol withdrawal
Endocrine and Metabolic: low blood sugar or a sodium derangement
Congenital: subdural hematoma
checks.why: Low blood sugar and sodium abnormalities are metabolic causes and are among the first things checked in confusion. Benzodiazepines are drugs, alcohol withdrawal is a drug or toxin effect, and a subdural hematoma is trauma.

checks.q: A 55-year-old smoker with chest pain has the pain reproduced when you press on his sternum. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: Acute coronary syndrome is excluded and the pain is musculoskeletal
The finding is meaningless and should not be documented
The finding proves costochondritis
A musculoskeletal cause becomes more likely, but a coronary event is not excluded
checks.why: Roughly 7 percent of patients with reproducible chest wall tenderness are still having a coronary event, so the finding shifts probability without excluding anything. It is worth documenting precisely because it shifts probability, and treating it as a rule-out is a classic lethal error.

lessons.title: Red flags by complaint
lessons.body:
## What a red flag is

A **red flag** is a feature that, when present, raises the probability of a dangerous cause enough to change what you do, usually from evaluate at the normal pace to escalate now. Red flags are not diagnoses. They are triggers.

This lesson is a reference. Learn the pattern first, because the same four things are flags in almost every complaint: **sudden onset, extremes of age, abnormal vital signs, and a focal neurologic deficit.**

### Chest pain

| Red flag | Worry |
|---|---|
| Exertional pressure with sweating, radiating to jaw or arm | Acute coronary syndrome |
| Tearing pain into the back, unequal arm pressures, pulse deficit | Aortic dissection |
| Pleuritic pain with sudden breathlessness, recent surgery, immobility, or cancer | Pulmonary embolism |
| Sudden pain with absent breath sounds on one side and low blood pressure | Tension pneumothorax |
| Pain after forceful vomiting, with crackling under the skin of the neck | Esophageal rupture |

### Headache

| Red flag | Worry |
|---|---|
| Maximal within seconds, worst of life | Subarachnoid hemorrhage |
| Fever with a stiff neck, rash, or altered mental status | Meningitis |
| New headache after age 50 with scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, vision loss | Temporal arteritis |
| Focal deficit, seizure, or headache worst in the morning with vomiting | Mass or bleed raising pressure inside the skull |
| Any head strike on blood thinners, or any headache after a fall in an older patient | Intracranial hemorrhage |

### Back pain

| Red flag | Worry |
|---|---|
| Numbness over the buttocks and inner thighs, urinary retention or incontinence, weakness in both legs | Cauda equina syndrome |
| Fever, injection drug use, recent spinal procedure, immunosuppression | Spinal epidural abscess |
| Age over 50 with tearing pain and a pulsatile abdominal mass | Abdominal aortic aneurysm |
| Cancer history, unexplained weight loss, pain that wakes them at night | Metastatic disease |

### Abdominal pain

| Red flag | Worry |
|---|---|
| Severe pain with a soft, unimpressive belly, often with atrial fibrillation | Mesenteric ischemia |
| Rigid abdomen, rebound, guarding | Perforation and peritonitis |
| Any woman of childbearing age with no pregnancy test done | Ectopic pregnancy |
| Elderly, diabetic, or immunosuppressed patient with vague pain and normal vitals | A catastrophe with a muted presentation |

### Fever

Fever is `38.0` C, which is `100.4` F. The flags are what comes with it.

- With a systolic under `100`, a respiratory rate of `22` or more, or new confusion: sepsis.
- With a new murmur, especially with injection drug use: endocarditis.
- With a stiff neck or a non-blanching purple rash: meningitis and meningococcemia.
- In a patient on chemotherapy: neutropenic fever, antibiotics within 60 minutes.
- With back pain: epidural abscess until proven otherwise.

### Dizziness

First make them choose: does the room spin, do you feel like you will pass out, or are you off balance. Then the flags: sudden vertigo with inability to walk unassisted, new headache or neck pain, double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, or any focal deficit point to a stroke in the back of the brain. Near-fainting during exertion, or a family history of sudden death, points at the heart.

### Shortness of breath

Oxygen saturation below `90%` on room air, respiratory rate over `30` or under `8`, one-word answers, tripod posture, accessory muscle use, new confusion, sudden onset, or a quiet chest in a known asthmatic, which means too little air is moving to make a wheeze.

### Fever in children

| Age or finding | Action |
|---|---|
| Under 28 days with a rectal temperature of `38.0` C or higher | Full sepsis evaluation, no exceptions for looking well |
| 1 to 3 months and ill appearing | Immediate provider evaluation |
| Any age with petechiae, a stiff neck, inconsolability, or a bulging soft spot | Meningitis until proven otherwise |
| Poor feeding, fewer than 3 wet diapers a day, no tears when crying | Dehydration |

### The elderly

Older patients hide disease. Fever is blunted, the heart rate cannot rise on a beta blocker, and the white count may be normal. A blood pressure of `120/70` may be shock in someone who lives at `165/90`. Heart attack presents as nausea or fatigue, pneumonia as confusion or a fall, infection as delirium, and a surgical abdomen can feel soft.

> **Key:** The same four flags repeat everywhere: sudden onset, extremes of age, abnormal vitals, focal neurologic deficit.

> **On shift:** A red flag belongs in the first sentence you say to someone, not in the middle of a story. "This is a 68-year-old with back pain who cannot feel the saddle area and has not urinated since last night."
keyPoints: Four flags repeat across nearly every complaint: sudden onset, extremes of age, abnormal vitals, focal neurologic deficit.
Chest pain killers are acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, dissection, tension pneumothorax, and esophageal rupture.
Cauda equina is saddle numbness, urinary retention or incontinence, and bilateral leg weakness, and it is time-critical.
Any fever of 38.0 C or higher in an infant under 28 days triggers a full sepsis evaluation regardless of appearance.
The elderly present atypically: heart attack as fatigue, pneumonia as a fall, infection as delirium, a surgical belly that feels soft.

checks.q: A 44-year-old says his headache hit maximum intensity within seconds while he was watching television, and is the worst he has ever had. What is the concern?
choices: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Tension headache from stress
Migraine without aura
Temporal arteritis
checks.why: Thunderclap onset, meaning maximal within about a minute, is the classic presentation of bleeding into the space around the brain. Tension headaches and migraines build over minutes to hours, and temporal arteritis is a subacute headache in patients over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing.

checks.q: Which combination in a patient with back pain requires immediate escalation?
choices: Pain worse with bending and better with rest
Numbness over the buttocks with new urinary retention and weakness in both legs
Muscle spasm palpable next to the spine
Pain that started after lifting a heavy box yesterday
checks.why: Saddle numbness, retention, and bilateral leg weakness are cauda equina syndrome, where delay costs permanent bowel, bladder, and sexual function. Mechanical pain, paraspinal spasm, and a lifting history are the ordinary pattern and carry no red flag by themselves.

checks.q: A 21-day-old infant has a rectal temperature of 38.2 C and is feeding well and smiling. What is the correct action?
choices: Advise fluids and recheck in 24 hours since the baby looks well
Give a weight-based dose of acetaminophen and discharge
Full sepsis evaluation, because appearance does not exclude serious infection at this age
Test only for respiratory viruses
checks.why: Under 28 days of age, a rectal temperature of 38.0 C or higher gets a full evaluation regardless of how well the infant looks, because newborns can be bacteremic or have meningitis while still feeding and smiling. Reassurance, fever reducers, or viral testing alone all rely on an appearance that is not reliable at this age.

lessons.title: Pretest probability and what a test actually tells you
lessons.body:
## A test does not tell you the truth, it moves a number

Before you order anything, you already have an estimate of how likely the disease is. That is the **pretest probability**, and it comes from who the patient is plus what the history and exam showed. A test takes that number and moves it up or down to a **post-test probability**. That is all a test does.

## Sensitivity and specificity

- **Sensitivity:** of the people who have the disease, the fraction the test catches. A sensitive test has few false negatives.
- **Specificity:** of the people who do not have the disease, the fraction the test correctly calls negative. A specific test has few false positives.

Two memory hooks that get used at the bedside:

- **SnNout.** A highly sensitive test, when negative, rules out.
- **SpPin.** A highly specific test, when positive, rules in.

## Predictive values depend on who is in front of you

Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. **Predictive values** are properties of the test in a particular population.

- **Positive predictive value:** if the test is positive, how likely is the disease to be real?
- **Negative predictive value:** if the test is negative, how likely is the patient to be truly disease-free?

Both move with **prevalence**. The identical test that is trustworthy in a chest pain unit full of high-risk patients produces mostly false positives in a walk-in clinic where almost nobody has the disease. Nothing about the test changed. The population did.

## Two worked examples

**D-dimer for pulmonary embolism.** Very sensitive, about `95%`, and poorly specific, roughly `40%` to `50%`. In a patient whose pretest probability is genuinely low, a negative D-dimer drops the post-test probability below the roughly `2%` threshold clinicians treat as done. In a patient with a high pretest probability, pleuritic pain, a fast heart rate, a swollen leg, a hip replacement three weeks ago, a negative D-dimer does not clear them and they go to imaging anyway. Same test, opposite meaning, because the starting number was different.

**Troponin for heart attack.** A raised troponin means heart muscle cells released protein. That happens in myocardial infarction, and also in pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney failure, heart failure, myocarditis, and after prolonged fast rhythms. A number is not a diagnosis. It is one input into a story.

> **Key:** Order a test when you already know what you will do for each possible result. If a positive and a negative lead to the same plan, do not order it.

## Likelihood ratios in one paragraph

A **likelihood ratio** compresses sensitivity and specificity into a single number: how much this result multiplies the odds of disease. Rough feel: `10` or higher is a big push toward the disease, `1` changes nothing, `0.1` or lower is a big push away. You do not need the arithmetic at the bedside. You need the idea that a result is a nudge of a certain size, not a verdict.

## Why ordering everything fails

Every test has a false positive rate. Run 20 independent tests on a healthy person, with the usual `95%` reference range, and on average about one comes back abnormal purely by chance. Each incidental finding buys more imaging, more radiation, more cost, more anxiety, and sometimes a biopsy of something that was never going to hurt anyone. Shotgun workups also stall the department, and the real diagnosis waits in line with everything else.

## Where the numbers come from

- A **guideline** is a body of experts summarizing many studies into a recommendation. It is where you start, not where you stop.
- A **randomized controlled trial** assigns treatment by chance, which is the only design that reliably separates cause from association.
- An **observational study** watches what already happened. It is cheaper and more realistic and cannot fully exclude confounding. Coffee drinkers living longer is an association, not a prescription.
- **Number needed to treat** is how many patients must receive a treatment for one to benefit. **Number needed to harm** is how many before one is harmed. An NNT of `5` is a powerful drug; an NNT of `200` is a population-level effect you will never notice in one patient.
- **One study does not change practice.** Single trials get contradicted constantly. Practice moves when a result replicates and a guideline body adopts it.

> **On shift:** The lookup habit is normal behavior, not a confession. UpToDate for the deep dive, the specialty guideline for what counts as standard, and a bedside reference such as MDCalc or WikEM for a score or a dose.
keyPoints: A test moves a pretest probability to a post-test probability; it does not deliver truth.
Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test; predictive values belong to the population and move with prevalence.
SnNout: a sensitive test when negative rules out. SpPin: a specific test when positive rules in.
A negative D-dimer excludes pulmonary embolism only when pretest probability was already low; a raised troponin has many non-cardiac causes.
Order a test only when a positive and a negative would lead to different plans.

checks.q: A patient has pleuritic chest pain, a heart rate of 112, a swollen right calf, and a knee replacement 10 days ago. The D-dimer comes back negative. What does that mean?
choices: Pulmonary embolism is excluded, because D-dimer is highly sensitive
The pretest probability was high, so a negative D-dimer does not exclude embolism and imaging is still needed
The test must have been run incorrectly and should be repeated
A negative D-dimer is meaningless in every patient
checks.why: A negative result from a sensitive test lowers probability by a fixed amount, and from a high starting point that is not enough to get under the threshold for stopping. In a genuinely low-risk patient the same result would exclude the disease, which is precisely what makes pretest probability the deciding factor. Repeating the test does not change the starting number.

checks.q: The same test is used in an emergency department where 20 percent of patients have the disease and in a screening clinic where 1 percent do. What changes?
choices: Sensitivity falls in the clinic
Specificity rises in the clinic
The positive predictive value falls in the clinic, so more positives are false
Nothing changes, because test characteristics are fixed
checks.why: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and stay put. Predictive values depend on prevalence, so in a low-prevalence setting a positive result is much more likely to be a false positive. That is the whole reason screening low-risk populations generates so much unnecessary follow-up.

checks.q: A drug for a common condition has a number needed to treat of 180 and a number needed to harm of 90. What is the plainest reading?
choices: You would harm one patient for every 90 treated and benefit one for every 180, so harm outweighs benefit at these numbers
The drug helps twice as many people as it hurts
The numbers cannot be compared to each other
An NNT of 180 means 180 percent of patients improve
checks.why: Smaller numbers mean the event happens more often, so an NNH of 90 is more frequent than an NNT of 180. The comparison is exactly what these numbers exist for, though the severity of the harm versus the benefit still matters. NNT is a count of patients, never a percentage.

lessons.title: Clinical decision rules worth knowing cold
lessons.body:
## What a rule is for

A **clinical decision rule** turns findings into a number that has been tested on thousands of patients, so that a decision performs at least as well as an expert's gut and can be defended in writing. Rules do not replace judgment. They document it.

Two cautions first. A rule only applies in the population it was built in, so the pulmonary embolism rules assume you are already considering embolism. And low risk is a probability, never a promise.

### HEART score, for chest pain

Five parts, each scored `0` to `2`, total `0` to `10`.

| Part | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| History | slightly suspicious | moderately suspicious | highly suspicious |
| ECG | normal | non-specific changes | significant ST deviation |
| Age | under 45 | 45 to 64 | 65 or older |
| Risk factors | none | 1 to 2 | 3 or more, or known vascular disease |
| Troponin | normal | 1 to 3 times normal | over 3 times normal |

`0` to `3` is low risk, roughly `1%` to `2%` chance of a major cardiac event in the next 6 weeks, generally dischargeable with follow-up. `4` to `6` is moderate, meaning observation with repeat troponins. `7` to `10` is high, meaning admission with cardiology.

### Wells for pulmonary embolism, and PERC

Wells points: signs of a deep vein clot `3`, embolism is the most likely diagnosis `3`, heart rate over `100` `1.5`, immobilization or surgery in the past 4 weeks `1.5`, previous clot `1.5`, coughing blood `1`, cancer `1`. A common split is `4` or less means unlikely, so get a D-dimer, and over `4` means likely, so image.

**PERC** is the rule that lets you stop without even a D-dimer, but only when your own pretest probability is already under about `15%`. All eight must be negative:

1. Age under 50
2. Heart rate under `100`
3. Oxygen saturation on room air `95%` or higher
4. No swelling of one leg only
5. No coughing of blood
6. No surgery or trauma needing hospitalization in the past 4 weeks
7. No previous deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
8. No hormone use, meaning oral contraceptives or hormone replacement

### Wells for deep vein thrombosis

One point each for active cancer, paralysis or recent immobilization of the leg, bedridden 3 days or surgery within 12 weeks, tenderness along the deep veins, the whole leg swollen, a calf more than `3 cm` larger than the other side, pitting edema on the symptomatic side, collateral surface veins, and a previous clot. Subtract `2` if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely. `0` or less is low, `1` to `2` moderate, `3` or more high.

### Ottawa ankle and knee rules

Ankle films only for pain in the malleolar zone with bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps both at the scene and in the department. The companion Ottawa foot rule sends a midfoot injury for foot films if there is tenderness at the navicular or at the base of the fifth metatarsal, or the same inability to take four steps. Knee films for age 55 or older, isolated kneecap tenderness, tenderness at the head of the fibula, inability to bend to 90 degrees, or inability to take four steps. These approach `100%` sensitivity for important fracture and cut x-rays by roughly a third.

### Head and neck

- **Canadian CT head rule.** For minor head injury with a GCS of 13 to 15 plus loss of consciousness, amnesia, or disorientation. High-risk features: GCS under 15 two hours after injury, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, any sign of basilar skull fracture, vomiting twice or more, age 65 or older.
- **NEXUS.** No cervical spine imaging if all five are true: no midline neck tenderness, no focal neurologic deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no painful distracting injury.
- **Canadian C-spine rule.** A three-step alternative adding dangerous mechanism and the ability to turn the head 45 degrees each way.
- **PECARN.** The pediatric head injury rule identifying children at very low risk, so they can be observed rather than scanned. Know it exists and that pediatric CT is avoided whenever it safely can be.

### Infection and severity

- **CURB-65** for pneumonia, one point each: Confusion, blood Urea nitrogen over `19 mg/dL`, Respiratory rate `30` or more, Blood pressure with systolic under `90` or diastolic `60` or less, and age `65` or older. `0` to `1` is usually outpatient, `2` means consider admission, `3` or more means admit and consider intensive care.
- **Centor, modified by McIsaac,** for sore throat: one point each for fever, tonsillar exudate, tender front-of-neck nodes, and absence of cough, plus one for age 3 to 14 and minus one for age 45 or older. Low scores need no testing; higher scores get a rapid strep test.
- **SIRS.** Two or more of temperature over `38` C or under `36` C, heart rate over `90`, respiratory rate over `20`, white count over `12,000` or under `4,000`.
- **qSOFA.** Two or more of respiratory rate `22` or more, altered mental status, systolic blood pressure `100` or less. A bedside warning flag for sepsis with poor outcomes, not a diagnosis.
- **NIH Stroke Scale.** A `0` to `42` severity score guiding and following stroke treatment. Higher is worse, and roughly `5` or more is generally treated as a significant deficit.

> **Trap:** A score supports a decision, it does not make one. A PERC-negative patient who still looks wrong gets worked up anyway, and that override gets written down with the reason.
keyPoints: HEART is History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin, each 0 to 2; 0 to 3 low, 4 to 6 moderate, 7 to 10 high.
PERC has eight criteria and may only be applied when your own pretest probability is already under about 15 percent.
NEXUS clears the cervical spine on five findings; Ottawa rules decide ankle and knee films and are close to 100 percent sensitive for important fractures.
CURB-65 guides pneumonia disposition; qSOFA and SIRS flag possible sepsis but do not diagnose it.
A rule only applies in the population it was derived in, and an override is legitimate as long as it is documented with a reason.

checks.q: A 62-year-old with two cardiac risk factors has a moderately suspicious history, non-specific ECG changes, and a normal troponin. What is his HEART score and the usual pathway?
choices: Score 4, moderate risk, observation with repeat troponins
Score 2, low risk, immediate discharge with no follow-up needed
Score 8, high risk, admit to cardiology
Score 6, high risk, cardiac catheterization tonight
checks.why: History 1, ECG 1, age 62 gives 1, risk factors 1 to 2 gives 1, troponin normal gives 0, so the total is 4. That lands in the moderate band of 4 to 6, which means observation and serial troponins rather than discharge. High risk starts at 7.

checks.q: A 38-year-old has pleuritic chest pain. Your gut pretest probability for pulmonary embolism is roughly 10 percent, and all eight PERC criteria are negative. What is the next step?
choices: Order a CT pulmonary angiogram regardless
Order a D-dimer to confirm the PERC result
No further testing for embolism is required, because PERC applies at this pretest probability
Admit for serial D-dimers over 24 hours
checks.why: PERC was designed for exactly this situation: a low pretest probability, under about 15 percent, with all eight criteria negative, where further testing causes more harm than it prevents. Adding a D-dimer here produces false positives that drag the patient into a contrast CT, and imaging or admission would be even more aggressive.

checks.q: Which patient may have the cervical spine cleared by NEXUS without imaging?
choices: An alert, sober patient with no midline neck tenderness, no deficit, and a badly broken femur
A patient with normal alertness, no intoxication, no midline tenderness, no deficit, and no distracting injury
A patient who smells of alcohol but reports no neck pain
A confused elderly patient with no neck tenderness
checks.why: All five NEXUS criteria must be satisfied. A femur fracture is a painful distracting injury, intoxication invalidates the exam, and confusion fails the normal alertness criterion, so each of those patients needs imaging or a different rule.

lessons.title: The note: SOAP, decision making, and reading other people's reports
lessons.body:
## Why the note exists

The chart is four things at once: the plan for whoever sees this patient next, the record of what you were thinking, the bill, and the legal document. Years later in a deposition, the note is the only version of the encounter that still exists. The old rule is blunt and accurate: if it was not documented, it did not happen.

## SOAP

**Subjective** is what the patient tells you. **Objective** is what you measured and observed, with no interpretation. **Assessment** is your read, including the differential with a reason for each item. **Plan** is what you did, what you will do, and where the patient goes.

### A worked chest pain note

**S:** 58-year-old man, "pressure in my chest" for 3 hours, began while carrying groceries up stairs, `6/10`, under the breastbone, radiating to the left jaw, with sweating and nausea. Eased slightly with rest, unchanged by position or pressing. Denies fever, cough, leg swelling, or tearing pain to the back. High blood pressure, high cholesterol, 30 pack-year smoker. Medications lisinopril and atorvastatin. No allergies. Father had a heart attack at 52.

**O:** `T 36.8 C, HR 92, BP 156/94 right arm and 152/90 left arm, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air`. Alert, uncomfortable, skin cool and damp. Lungs clear. Heart regular, no murmur. Chest wall not tender. Abdomen soft. Legs without swelling or calf tenderness, pulses equal. ECG: sinus rhythm with `1 mm` ST depression in V4 through V6, no prior for comparison. Troponin `0.04 ng/mL`, upper limit `0.03`.

**A:** 58-year-old man with cardiac risk factors and 3 hours of exertional substernal pressure with radiation and sweating, lateral ST depression, and a mildly raised troponin. HEART score `8`. Most consistent with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. Dissection considered: no tearing pain, arm pressures within `4 mmHg`, no pulse deficit. Pulmonary embolism considered: no low oxygen, no leg findings, no immobilization. Pneumonia and chest wall pain do not fit.

**P:** Aspirin `324 mg` chewed, cardiac monitoring, IV access, repeat troponin and ECG in 3 hours, cardiology consulted, admit to telemetry on the NSTEMI pathway. Discussed with the patient and his wife.

## Medical decision making

The **medical decision making** section is where a note earns its keep. It has to show three things: the number and complexity of problems considered, the data you reviewed and why, and the risk of both the condition and the treatment. In practice that means writing down the thinking you already did, which killers you considered, what argued against them, and why this disposition. "Chest pain, admit" is not decision making. The assessment paragraph above is.

## Discharge instructions and return precautions

Written for the patient, not for the chart. Aim at a sixth-grade reading level, no abbreviations, four parts:

1. What we think is going on, in plain words.
2. What to do, including medicine name, dose, how often, and for how long.
3. Who to follow up with, by when, and how to reach them.
4. **Return precautions:** the specific things that mean come back now.

A real one sounds like this: "Come back right away if the pain returns while you are resting, if it lasts more than 15 minutes, if you become short of breath, if you faint, or if you start sweating with it."

> **Key:** Return precautions are the safety net for everything the workup could not exclude. They are the most important paragraph in a discharge and the one most often left as boilerplate.

## Reading other people's notes

A **consult note** has the same skeleton: reason for consultation, their focused history and exam, their impression, and their recommendations. Read the last two first, then check whether their history matches yours, because a consultant working from a wrong premise gives a confident wrong answer.

A **radiology report** has a fixed shape: clinical indication, technique, comparison, findings, then **impression**. The impression is the answer; the findings are the raw material. Radiologists hedge in a standard vocabulary, and the hedging carries meaning.

| Phrase | What it means |
|---|---|
| No acute intracranial abnormality | Nothing urgent is visible; this is not the same as a normal brain |
| Cannot exclude | This study is not good enough to answer that question |
| Clinical correlation recommended | The image is ambiguous and the decision belongs to the treating clinician |
| Recommend further imaging with | Get the other study; this is a real recommendation, not a formality |
| Compared with the prior study | The comparison is the finding, and no prior means less certainty |

> **On shift:** If a radiology impression changes anything about a patient's care, it gets told to the provider out loud, not left in the chart to be discovered.
keyPoints: Subjective is what they tell you, Objective is what you measure with no interpretation, Assessment carries the differential with reasons, Plan includes the disposition.
Medical decision making must show the problems considered, the data reviewed and why, and the risk of the condition and treatment.
Discharge instructions have four parts, and return precautions must name specific triggers rather than say come back if worse.
In a radiology report the impression is the answer and the findings are the raw data.
Hedged radiology language is meaningful: cannot exclude means the study cannot answer it, and clinical correlation recommended puts the decision back on you.

checks.q: Which entry belongs in the Objective section rather than anywhere else?
choices: Patient reports the pain is worse when he lies flat
Blood pressure 156/94 in the right arm, chest wall non-tender, ECG with 1 mm ST depression in V4 through V6
Most consistent with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
Admit to telemetry and repeat troponin in 3 hours
checks.why: Objective holds measurements, exam findings, and results with no interpretation attached. What the patient reports is Subjective, the diagnostic read is Assessment, and the disposition is Plan. Mixing them makes the note impossible to audit later.

checks.q: A note reads in full: Assessment, chest pain. Plan, admit. What is the main deficiency?
choices: It fails to show the problems considered, the data reviewed, and the risk, so no decision making is documented
It is too short to be billable, which is the primary problem
It should have used OLDCARTS instead of OPQRST
It omits the patient's family history
checks.why: The medical decision making section exists to show which dangerous diagnoses were considered, what data was reviewed and why, and what risk justified the disposition. Billing follows from that documentation rather than being the point of it, and the mnemonic used or a family history line would not fix an assessment that contains no reasoning.

checks.q: A head CT report ends with: no acute intracranial abnormality, clinical correlation recommended. What does that tell you?
choices: The brain is normal and no further concern is warranted
The radiologist believes the patient has a stroke
Nothing urgent is visible on this study, and the clinical decision still rests with the treating clinician
A repeat CT must be ordered in 6 hours
checks.why: No acute abnormality means nothing urgent was seen on this particular study, which is narrower than a normal brain, and early ischemic stroke is frequently invisible on an initial non-contrast CT. Clinical correlation recommended puts the decision back with the person who has the history, and it is not itself an order for repeat imaging.

lessons.title: Presenting, disposition, and consent
lessons.body:
## The one-liner

Every presentation opens with one sentence that orients the listener: **age, sex, the history that matters here, the complaint, and the duration.**

"58-year-old man with high blood pressure and a 30 pack-year smoking history, here with 3 hours of exertional chest pressure."

That sentence tells the listener which illness scripts to load. Leave the irrelevant history out. His 1998 appendectomy does not belong in it.

## Sixty seconds, in order

1. The one-liner
2. The history of present illness in chronological order, with pertinent positives and negatives
3. The past history, medications, and allergies that matter for this problem
4. Vital signs and the pertinent exam
5. Results you already have
6. Assessment: your leading diagnosis and two alternatives
7. Plan, and the question you actually have

Do not read the chart front to back. The listener is assembling a picture and needs the pieces in that order.

## The audience changes the content

- **To a nurse:** what changed and what you need. "Room 12's heart rate went from 88 to 130 and he looks gray. Do you want him on the monitor?"
- **To a provider:** the full structure above, ending in a specific request.
- **To a consultant:** the reason for the call first, then the story. "I am calling about a 58-year-old with an NSTEMI, troponin `0.4`, on heparin. I need to know whether you want him in the catheterization lab tonight."

## SBAR

For escalation: **Situation** (who, where, what is wrong now), **Background** (the relevant history in one sentence), **Assessment** (what you think is happening), **Recommendation** (what you want).

The phrase that makes SBAR work is **"I'm worried because."** It converts a report into an escalation, and hospital safety programs deliberately protect it so anyone at any level can use it. "I'm worried because his rate keeps climbing and his pressure is drifting down."

> **Key:** If you cannot say what you want, you have not escalated. End with a request.

## Disposition

Every emergency patient ends in one of three buckets.

- **Admit.** Needs treatment or monitoring that only the hospital provides.
- **Observe.** Needs a defined short course, such as serial troponins or a few hours of a medication drip, with a decision at the end of it.
- **Discharge.** Safe to continue at home.

Safe to go home is a checklist, not a feeling: the killers considered and excluded, pain and vital signs acceptable, able to walk and keep fluids down, has the medicine and can afford it, has a ride and a place to go, has a real follow-up, and understands the return precautions. The medicine can be perfect and the disposition still unsafe if the patient lives alone at the top of three flights of stairs in a new knee immobilizer.

**Shared decision making** is the honest version of a borderline call. Give the risk in numbers, lay out the options, decide together. "Your HEART score is 3, about a 2 percent chance of a heart problem over the next 6 weeks. You can stay for repeat blood work, or go home and see cardiology this week. Here is what each looks like."

## Capacity, consent, and leaving against advice

The four principles in plain words: **autonomy** (their choice), **beneficence** (do good), **nonmaleficence** (do no harm), **justice** (fair treatment and fair use of resources).

**Capacity** is decision-specific, clinical, and assessed at the bedside. The patient must be able to:

1. **Understand** the information
2. **Appreciate** that it applies to them
3. **Reason** with it, weighing the options against each other
4. **Express** a consistent choice

Competence, by contrast, is a legal status decided by a court. Intoxication, delirium, and a drop in mental status can remove capacity temporarily, and capacity is judged for this decision at this moment, not in general.

**Informed consent** requires the diagnosis, the proposed treatment, its risks and benefits, the alternatives with their risks and benefits, and the consequences of refusing, all in language the patient understands, with a voluntary choice at the end.

The exceptions: the **emergency exception**, sometimes called implied consent, covers a patient who cannot consent and faces a serious threat to life or limb. **Minors** need a parent or guardian, except emancipated minors and, in most states, care for pregnancy, sexually transmitted infection, substance use, and mental health. When a patient lacks capacity, a **surrogate** decides, in a legally defined order that usually runs healthcare proxy, then spouse, then adult children, then parents.

A **DNR** or a **POLST** form limits specific interventions, usually intubation and chest compressions. It does not mean do not treat. Comfort-focused care is an active plan: oxygen, pain control, antinausea medicine, positioning, and family at the bedside.

**Leaving against medical advice,** done right: assess and document capacity, state the specific risk in plain words ("you could have a heart attack tonight and die"), offer whatever care they will accept, give the prescriptions and the follow-up anyway, write real return precautions, and tell them they can come back.

> **Trap:** An AMA signature is not a legal shield. The documented capacity assessment and the specific risks you explained are what protect the patient and the chart.
keyPoints: The one-liner is age, sex, relevant history, complaint, duration, and it tells the listener which illness scripts to load.
Present in order: one-liner, HPI, relevant history, vitals and pertinent exam, results, assessment with alternatives, plan and your question.
Consultants want the question first; nurses want what changed and what you need; SBAR ends in a recommendation.
Safe to go home is a checklist covering medicine, mobility, transport, housing, follow-up, and return precautions, not a feeling.
Capacity has four components and is decision-specific and clinical, while competence is a legal determination made by a court.

checks.q: You call the on-call surgeon about a patient. Which opening is most effective?
choices: A chronological account starting with the patient's childhood surgeries
I am calling about a 24-year-old with right lower quadrant pain and a CT showing appendicitis; I need to know when you can see her
I have a patient here who is in a lot of pain and I am not sure what to do
Reading the full nursing note aloud from the beginning
checks.why: Consultants want the reason for the call and the specific question first, then the story. A long chronology or a full nursing note buries the ask, and an open-ended statement of uncertainty gives the consultant nothing to act on.

checks.q: A patient's blood pressure is drifting down and you want the provider at the bedside. Which SBAR element is most often left out, and which phrase fixes it?
choices: Background is left out, fixed by reciting the full past medical history
Situation is left out, fixed by describing the room number only
The recommendation is left out, and the phrase I'm worried because turns a report into an escalation
Assessment is left out, fixed by waiting for the next set of vitals
checks.why: Most failed escalations are reports without a request, so the missing piece is the recommendation. Saying you are worried and naming why is the protected language that makes the concern actionable, while waiting for another set of vitals is the delay the escalation exists to prevent.

checks.q: A man with chest pain and an abnormal ECG wants to leave. He is alert, explains his diagnosis back to you, describes the risk of dying tonight, weighs it against needing to get home, and states his choice consistently. What is the correct approach?
choices: He lacks capacity because the choice is unwise, so he may be held
He has capacity; document the assessment and the specific risks discussed, offer what he will accept, give prescriptions, follow-up, and return precautions
Have him sign the AMA form, which is sufficient legal protection on its own
Call security, since any patient who refuses cardiac care is a danger to himself
checks.why: He demonstrates all four components of capacity, and an unwise choice made with capacity is still his to make. The signature alone protects nothing; the documented capacity assessment and the specific risks explained are what matter, and holding or restraining a patient with capacity is false imprisonment.

cards.front: What are the three parts of an illness script?
cards.back: Who gets it (epidemiology and risk factors), what it does to the body and how fast (mechanism and time course), and what it looks like (key features, including the findings that should not be there).

cards.front: What is the difference between System 1 and System 2 reasoning?
cards.back: System 1 is fast automatic pattern matching against stored illness scripts. System 2 is slow, deliberate, one-fact-at-a-time analysis. System 1 generates candidates, System 2 verifies them.

cards.front: When does fast pattern recognition most often fail?
cards.back: On atypical presentations, such as a heart attack showing up as nausea in a diabetic or pneumonia showing up as confusion in an 82-year-old, and when the clinician is tired, rushed, interrupted, or emotionally loaded about the patient.

cards.front: Name three concrete inputs to the sick or not sick gestalt.
cards.back: The doorway impression (color, work of breathing, posture, ability to finish a sentence), the vital sign trend rather than one set, and mismatches such as pain out of proportion to the exam.

cards.front: Why is a heart rate of 96, then 108, then 124 worth reporting even when the blood pressure is normal?
cards.back: It is compensated shock. The body defends pressure by speeding the heart, so by the time the systolic falls, compensation has already failed. Trends beat single snapshots.

cards.front: What five lines belong in a de-identified case log entry?
cards.back: Chief complaint, what was ordered, what it showed, the disposition, and one thing learned. No names, no dates of birth, no identifiers.

cards.front: What is anchoring bias, with an emergency department example?
cards.back: Fixing on the first piece of information and reading everything through it. Example: treating a triage label of anxiety attack in a panting 34-year-old and missing the pulmonary embolism after a long flight.

cards.front: What is premature closure, with an example?
cards.back: Stopping the diagnostic search once an answer fits. Example: flank pain with blood in the urine called a kidney stone in a 68-year-old smoker who actually has a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm.

cards.front: What is availability bias, and how does it work in reverse?
cards.back: Judging likelihood by what comes to mind easily, usually what you saw recently or vividly. In reverse, a disease you have never personally seen simply does not occur to you.

cards.front: What is diagnosis momentum?
cards.back: A label applied early by family, EMS, or triage hardening into accepted fact as it is handed along, with nobody re-examining the original evidence. Example: a family calling it a seizure when it was ventricular tachycardia.

cards.front: What is the frequent flyer or attribution bias, and why is it dangerous?
cards.back: Explaining a complaint away by the patient's identity or thick chart. Dangerous because these patients carry more disease than average, not less. Example: the familiar intoxicated patient with a new subdural hematoma.

cards.front: Name the three debiasing habits and what each one asks.
cards.back: The diagnostic time-out: working diagnosis, what does not fit, worst case. Forcing alternatives: what else could this be, name two. Worst-first: exclude the killers before naming the likely diagnosis.

cards.front: How should a chief complaint be written?
cards.back: One line in the patient's own words with a duration, such as chest pressure for 2 hours. Not a hypothesis like rule out MI. The patient's adjective carries diagnostic information.

cards.front: What does OPQRST stand for?
cards.back: Onset, Provocation and palliation, Quality, Radiation, Severity from 0 to 10 now and at worst, and Timing. It is built for pain.

cards.front: What does OLDCARTS stand for and when do you use it?
cards.back: Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating and Alleviating factors, Radiation, Timing, Severity. Used for complaints that are not primarily pain.

cards.front: What is a pertinent negative and why does it matter?
cards.back: A symptom you asked about because of your differential and recorded as absent. It is evidence, and it proves on paper which dangerous diagnoses you considered.

cards.front: Why must every allergy be recorded with the reaction?
cards.back: Penicillin with hives is an allergy; penicillin with an upset stomach is a side effect. The distinction decides whether an entire antibiotic class stays available.

cards.front: In what order is the abdomen examined, and why that order?
cards.back: Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate, with the tender area last. Pressing first alters bowel sounds and makes the patient guard against the rest of the exam.

cards.front: How does a focused emergency H and P differ from a full admission H and P?
cards.back: The emergency version is hypothesis-driven: focused history, the past history that changes management now, and the exam that excludes the killers. The admission version is complete, because that team owns the patient for days.

cards.front: What are the three rankings inside a differential diagnosis?
cards.back: Must not miss (kills if missed, so excluded first), most likely (highest probability for this patient), and most treatable (where finding it changes management now). A good plan handles all three.

cards.front: How do you build a differential from anatomy?
cards.back: Walk the layers and organs of the region from outside in. Right upper quadrant: skin and wall, ribs and muscle, pleura and lung base, liver, gallbladder and ducts, duodenum, head of pancreas, right kidney, hepatic flexure.

cards.front: What does VINDICATE stand for?
cards.back: Vascular, Infectious, Neoplastic, Degenerative and Drugs, Iatrogenic and Idiopathic, Congenital, Autoimmune, Trauma and Toxins, Endocrine and Metabolic. A category checklist for confusing presentations.

cards.front: Does chest pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall exclude a heart attack?
cards.back: No. It shifts probability toward a musculoskeletal cause, but roughly 7 percent of patients with reproducible chest wall tenderness are still having a coronary event.

cards.front: What is the three-item differential habit?
cards.back: Name three diagnoses with one reason each, plus one honest outlier and the specific thing you would check for it. Short enough to say in a hallway, complete enough to act on.

cards.front: Which four red flags repeat across nearly every chief complaint?
cards.back: Sudden onset, extremes of age, abnormal vital signs, and a focal neurologic deficit.

cards.front: Name the five must-not-miss causes of chest pain.
cards.back: Acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, and esophageal rupture. Pericardial tamponade is the sixth commonly added.

cards.front: Which headache features are red flags?
cards.back: Maximal within seconds (thunderclap), fever with stiff neck or rash, new headache after 50 with scalp tenderness or jaw pain on chewing, focal deficit or seizure, and any headache on blood thinners.

cards.front: What triad signals cauda equina syndrome in a patient with back pain?
cards.back: Numbness over the buttocks and inner thighs, urinary retention or incontinence, and weakness in both legs. It is time-critical, since delay costs permanent bowel, bladder, and sexual function.

cards.front: What is the rule for fever in an infant under 28 days old?
cards.back: A rectal temperature of 38.0 C, which is 100.4 F, or higher triggers a full sepsis evaluation, with no exception for a well-appearing baby.

cards.front: Why do elderly patients hide serious illness?
cards.back: Fever is blunted, beta blockers prevent tachycardia, and the white count may be normal. Heart attack presents as nausea or fatigue, pneumonia as confusion or a fall, infection as delirium, and a surgical abdomen can feel soft.

cards.front: Define sensitivity and specificity in one sentence each.
cards.back: Sensitivity: of people who have the disease, the fraction the test catches, so few false negatives. Specificity: of people without the disease, the fraction correctly called negative, so few false positives.

cards.front: What do SnNout and SpPin mean?
cards.back: SnNout: a highly sensitive test, when negative, rules the disease out. SpPin: a highly specific test, when positive, rules it in.

cards.front: Why do predictive values change from one setting to another?
cards.back: Positive and negative predictive value depend on prevalence. The same test that is trustworthy where disease is common produces mostly false positives where almost nobody has it.

cards.front: Why does a negative D-dimer rule out pulmonary embolism only in a low-risk patient?
cards.back: D-dimer is about 95 percent sensitive but only 40 to 50 percent specific. From a low starting probability a negative result falls below the roughly 2 percent stopping threshold; from a high starting point it does not, so the patient is imaged.

cards.front: Name five causes of a raised troponin that are not a heart attack.
cards.back: Pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney failure, heart failure, and myocarditis. Prolonged fast rhythms and cardiac contusion also do it. Troponin means myocardial injury, not a mechanism.

cards.front: What does a likelihood ratio tell you, and what do 10, 1, and 0.1 mean?
cards.back: How much a result multiplies the odds of disease. About 10 or higher is a big push toward the disease, 1 changes nothing, and 0.1 or lower is a big push away.

cards.front: What single question should be answered before ordering any test?
cards.back: What will I do differently for each possible result? If a positive and a negative lead to the same plan, the test is not indicated.

cards.front: What do number needed to treat and number needed to harm mean?
cards.back: NNT is how many patients must receive a treatment for one to benefit; NNH is how many before one is harmed. An NNT of 5 is a powerful drug, an NNT of 200 is a population-level effect.

cards.front: What are the five components of the HEART score?
cards.back: History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin, each scored 0 to 2, for a total of 0 to 10.

cards.front: What are the HEART score bands and what does each mean?
cards.back: 0 to 3 low risk, roughly 1 to 2 percent major cardiac events, generally dischargeable with follow-up. 4 to 6 moderate, observation with repeat troponins. 7 to 10 high, admit with cardiology.

cards.front: What are the highest-weighted items in the Wells score for pulmonary embolism?
cards.back: Clinical signs of a deep vein clot and embolism being the most likely diagnosis, at 3 points each. Heart rate over 100, recent immobilization or surgery, and a previous clot are 1.5 each.

cards.front: List the eight PERC criteria.
cards.back: Age under 50, heart rate under 100, room-air oxygen saturation 95 percent or higher, no one-sided leg swelling, no coughing of blood, no surgery or trauma in 4 weeks, no prior clot, and no hormone use.

cards.front: When may the PERC rule be applied at all?
cards.back: Only when your own pretest probability for pulmonary embolism is already under about 15 percent. In a higher-risk patient, a negative PERC does not exclude embolism.

cards.front: What does the Ottawa ankle rule require before an x-ray?
cards.back: Malleolar-zone pain with bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps both at the scene and in the department. The navicular and the base of the fifth metatarsal belong to the companion Ottawa foot rule, which orders foot films.

cards.front: What are the five NEXUS criteria?
cards.back: No midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurologic deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no painful distracting injury. All five must be satisfied to skip cervical spine imaging.

cards.front: What does CURB-65 stand for and what do the scores mean?
cards.back: Confusion, blood Urea nitrogen over 19 mg/dL, Respiratory rate 30 or more, Blood pressure with systolic under 90 or diastolic 60 or less, and age 65 or older. 0 to 1 outpatient, 2 consider admission, 3 or more admit.

cards.front: What are the qSOFA criteria, and what does a positive score mean?
cards.back: Respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mental status, systolic blood pressure 100 mmHg or less. Two or more flags a patient at risk of poor sepsis outcomes. It is a warning, not a diagnosis.

cards.front: What goes in each letter of SOAP?
cards.back: Subjective: what the patient tells you. Objective: what you measured and observed, without interpretation. Assessment: the one-liner, working diagnosis, and differential with reasons. Plan: what you did, will do, and the disposition.

cards.front: What three things must a medical decision making section show?
cards.back: The number and complexity of problems considered, the data reviewed and why, and the risk of both the condition and the treatment. In practice: which killers you considered and what argued against them.

cards.front: What four parts belong in written discharge instructions?
cards.back: What we think is going on in plain words, the medicine with dose and duration, who to follow up with and by when, and specific return precautions.

cards.front: Why are return precautions the most important paragraph in a discharge?
cards.back: They are the safety net for everything the workup could not exclude. They must name specific triggers, such as return if the pain comes back at rest or lasts more than 15 minutes.

cards.front: What is the structure of a radiology report, and which part is the answer?
cards.back: Clinical indication, technique, comparison, findings, then impression. The impression is the answer; the findings are the raw data.

cards.front: What belongs in a patient one-liner?
cards.back: Age, sex, the history that matters for this problem, the chief complaint, and the duration. It tells the listener which illness scripts to load.

cards.front: What is the order of a 60-second patient presentation?
