cards.back: One-liner, history of present illness in order with pertinent positives and negatives, relevant history and medications, vitals and pertinent exam, results, assessment with two alternatives, plan and your specific question.

cards.front: How does presenting to a consultant differ from presenting to a provider?
cards.back: Lead with why you are calling and the question you need answered, then give the story. Consultants want the ask first; other listeners want the story first.

cards.front: What does SBAR stand for, and which phrase makes it work?
cards.back: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The phrase is I'm worried because, which converts a report into an escalation. Always end with what you want.

cards.front: What are the four components of decision-making capacity?
cards.back: Understand the information, appreciate that it applies to them, reason with it by comparing options, and express a consistent choice. Capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is legal.

cards.front: What are the five elements of informed consent?
cards.back: The diagnosis, the proposed treatment, its risks and benefits, the alternatives with their risks and benefits, and the consequences of refusing, in understandable language with a voluntary choice.

cards.front: What makes an against-medical-advice discharge defensible?
cards.back: A documented capacity assessment and the specific risks explained in plain words, plus offering what the patient will accept, giving prescriptions and follow-up, real return precautions, and an invitation to return. The signature alone is not a shield.

quiz.q: A provider steps into a room, glances at the patient, and immediately asks for a 12-lead ECG and IV access before taking a history. Which statement about this reasoning is most accurate?
choices: It is System 1 pattern recognition, appropriate as a generator but requiring a deliberate check that the killers do not fit
It is System 2 analytic reasoning and should be applied to every patient in the department
It is a cognitive error, because no reasoning is valid before a complete history
It is acceptable for experienced clinicians and does not require later verification
quiz.why: Instant recognition from a glance is System 1 pattern matching, which is the normal and efficient first step; the safeguard is 30 seconds of deliberate checking afterward. System 2 is the slow mode and cannot be run on everyone. Calling early recognition an error ignores that it is the most reliable early signal available, and no one's pattern match is exempt from verification.

quiz.q: Which set of observations best supports a sick impression before any vital signs have been taken?
choices: A stated pain score of 10 out of 10 with a calm affect
Tripod posture, damp skin, and speech in two- or three-word bursts
A long list of chronic medications on the home list
A prior visit for the same complaint three weeks ago
quiz.why: Work of breathing, skin findings, and the inability to complete a sentence are physiologic and observable from the doorway. A pain score is subjective and tracks poorly with severity of illness, a medication list is history rather than a current finding, and a repeat visit is a reason for more suspicion but is not itself a physiologic sign.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old on metoprolol has serial vitals of HR 78 with BP 148/86, then HR 84 with BP 122/74, then HR 88 with BP 104/66. He says he feels a little off. What is the most accurate reading?
choices: Reassuring, since the heart rate never exceeds 100
An expected effect of his home blood pressure medication
A falling pressure with a blunted heart rate response, consistent with early shock in a beta-blocked patient
Measurement artifact, since each change is small
quiz.why: Beta blockers prevent the compensatory tachycardia you normally rely on, so a rate under 100 is not reassurance in this patient. A systolic dropping from 148 to 104 is a large relative fall in someone who lives hypertensive, and a home medication does not produce a progressive decline over one visit. Small consistent changes in the same direction paired with a symptom are signal, not artifact.

quiz.q: A 61-year-old woman with epigastric burning is labeled likely gastritis at triage, improves slightly with antacids, and is nearly discharged before an ECG shows an inferior STEMI. Which pair of biases best explains what happened?
choices: Availability and base-rate neglect
Confirmation bias and the sunk cost fallacy
Attribution bias and outcome bias
Anchoring and premature closure
quiz.why: The first label set the frame, which is anchoring, and the search stopped once an explanation appeared to fit, which is premature closure. Availability is over-weighting what was seen recently, attribution bias explains a complaint away by who the patient is, and outcome bias only operates after the result is known.

quiz.q: Which single question is the most effective bedside debiasing tool during a patient encounter?
choices: What else could this be?
Does the patient agree with my diagnosis?
Have I seen a case that looked like this before?
What is the most common cause of this symptom?
quiz.why: Forcing yourself to name alternatives is the technique that most consistently reduces diagnostic error. Asking whether you have seen it before actively recruits availability bias, reaching for the most common cause reinforces the pattern you are trying to test, and patient agreement is not a check on diagnostic accuracy.

quiz.q: A man well known to the department for alcohol-related visits arrives smelling of alcohol, sleepy but arousable, with a fresh scalp abrasion. The plan is a hallway bed until he sobers up. What is the strongest argument against that plan?
choices: Department policy requires admission for all patients with alcohol use disorder
His altered mental status has a second plausible cause, head injury, and his familiar history is lowering the evidence threshold without justification
Every intoxicated patient requires a head CT before disposition
He cannot be assessed in any way until he is completely sober
quiz.why: This is attribution bias: a familiar history is being used to explain away a finding with a dangerous alternative, and a scalp abrasion with depressed mental status raises subdural hematoma. There is no blanket policy requiring admission or imaging for intoxication, and serial reassessment rather than waiting passively for sobriety is how these patients are actually watched.

quiz.q: Which of the following is written correctly as a chief complaint?
choices: Rule out acute coronary syndrome
Patient is a poor historian
It feels like something is sitting on my chest, for 3 hours
Chest pain, likely musculoskeletal given the age
quiz.why: A chief complaint is the patient's own words plus a duration, and the exact adjective carries diagnostic information that a paraphrase loses. The first and last choices are hypotheses rather than complaints, and calling someone a poor historian records a judgment instead of any information.

quiz.q: A note for a 45-year-old with chest pain reads: positive for sweating and nausea; denies fever, cough, coughing blood, leg swelling, recent travel, or tearing pain to the back. What do the denials accomplish?
choices: They definitively exclude pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and aortic dissection
They satisfy a billing requirement and nothing more
They remove the need for a separate review of systems
They record which dangerous diagnoses were considered and supply evidence against them
quiz.why: Pertinent negatives are evidence and they display your differential on paper. They argue against pneumonia, embolism, and dissection but do not definitively exclude them, since exclusion requires a rule or a test. Billing is a byproduct, and pertinent negatives do not replace the review of systems.

quiz.q: Which sequence for the abdominal examination is correct, and for what reason?
choices: Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate, because pressing first alters bowel sounds and makes the patient guard
Palpate, inspect, auscultate, percuss, because the tender area should be identified first
Auscultate, palpate, inspect, percuss, because bowel sounds are the most reliable finding
Percuss, palpate, inspect, auscultate, because air-fluid levels must be identified first
quiz.why: Listening before touching preserves unaltered bowel sounds, and saving palpation for last, with the tender area last of all, keeps the remainder of the exam usable. Bowel sounds are in fact one of the weaker findings in abdominal pain, which is a reason not to destroy them for nothing, and once a patient guards you cannot get the earlier information back.

quiz.q: Why is a must-not-miss diagnosis addressed before the most likely diagnosis, even when its probability is low?
choices: Because it is statistically more common in an emergency department population
Because the cost of missing it is severe and irreversible, so it is excluded first regardless of probability
Because such diagnoses are faster and easier to exclude than common conditions
Because reimbursement rules require advanced imaging before any other testing
quiz.why: The ranking is driven by consequence, not frequency. Killers are generally less common and are often harder, not easier, to exclude, and the likely diagnosis is named only after the dangerous ones have been addressed. Billing rules play no part in the ordering.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old arrives confused with no obvious source. Working the VINDICATE categories, which pairing of category and cause is correct?
choices: Vascular: benzodiazepine overdose
Neoplastic: alcohol withdrawal
Endocrine and Metabolic: low blood sugar or a sodium derangement
Congenital: subdural hematoma
quiz.why: Low blood sugar and sodium abnormalities are metabolic causes and are among the very first things checked in new confusion, because both are common and both are immediately reversible. Benzodiazepines fall under drugs, alcohol withdrawal under drugs and toxins, and a subdural hematoma under trauma.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old smoker with 2 hours of substernal chest pressure has the pain partially reproduced when you press on his sternum. What is the correct conclusion to draw?
choices: Acute coronary syndrome is excluded and the pain is musculoskeletal
The finding is meaningless and should not be documented
The finding establishes costochondritis as the diagnosis
A musculoskeletal cause becomes somewhat more likely, but a coronary event is not excluded
quiz.why: Roughly 7 percent of patients with reproducible chest wall tenderness are having a coronary event anyway, so the finding shifts probability without excluding anything. It is worth documenting precisely because it shifts probability, and treating a single bedside finding as a rule-out for a killer is a classic and lethal error.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old reports a headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds while he sat watching television, and calls it the worst of his life. What is the leading concern?
choices: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Tension headache from stress
Migraine without aura
Temporal arteritis
quiz.why: Thunderclap onset, meaning maximal intensity within about a minute, is the classic presentation of bleeding into the space around the brain and is the reason this headache cannot simply be treated and discharged. Tension headaches and migraines build over minutes to hours, and temporal arteritis is a subacute headache in patients over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing.

quiz.q: Which combination in a patient with low back pain requires immediate escalation rather than routine evaluation?
choices: Pain worse with bending forward and relieved by rest
Numbness over the buttocks and inner thighs with new urinary retention and weakness in both legs
Palpable muscle spasm alongside the spine
Pain that began after lifting a heavy box the previous day
quiz.why: Saddle numbness, urinary retention, and bilateral leg weakness together are cauda equina syndrome, where delay costs permanent bowel, bladder, and sexual function. Mechanical pain, paraspinal spasm, and a lifting history describe the ordinary pattern and carry no red flag on their own.

quiz.q: A 19-day-old infant has a rectal temperature of 38.2 C, is feeding well, and smiles at his mother. What is the correct action?
choices: Advise fluids and recheck in 24 hours, since the baby looks well
Give weight-based acetaminophen and discharge with return precautions
Full sepsis evaluation, because appearance does not exclude serious infection at this age
Test for respiratory viruses only, and discharge if positive
quiz.why: Under 28 days, a rectal temperature of 38.0 C or higher triggers a full evaluation regardless of how well the infant appears, because newborns can be bacteremic or have meningitis while still feeding and smiling. Reassurance, a fever reducer, or viral testing alone all rely on an appearance that is simply not reliable at this age.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old woman on atenolol is brought in after a fall. She is confused, temperature 37.1 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 118/64, and her family says she normally runs around 165/90. Which interpretation is best?
choices: She is well, since all her vital signs fall within normal ranges
Confusion after a fall in this age group is almost always dementia progressing
The absence of fever effectively rules out infection at her age
Her vitals are falsely reassuring: fever is blunted, her beta blocker prevents tachycardia, and 118/64 may be relative hypotension for her
quiz.why: Each individual number sits in the normal range, but relative to her own baseline and her medications the picture is consistent with serious illness such as sepsis or an intracranial bleed. Elderly patients mount weaker fevers, beta blockers block the compensatory tachycardia, and attributing new confusion to dementia is the attribution error that misses reversible causes.

quiz.q: A patient has pleuritic chest pain, a heart rate of 112, a swollen right calf, and a knee replacement 10 days ago. His D-dimer returns negative. What does that result mean?
choices: The pretest probability was high, so a negative D-dimer does not exclude embolism and imaging is still required
Pulmonary embolism is excluded, because D-dimer is a highly sensitive test
The specimen was probably mishandled and the test should be repeated
A negative D-dimer carries no information in any patient
quiz.why: A negative result from a sensitive test lowers probability by a fixed amount, and starting from a high pretest probability that is not enough to fall under the threshold for stopping. In a genuinely low-risk patient the identical result would exclude the disease, which is exactly what makes pretest probability the deciding factor, and repeating the test does not change the starting number.

quiz.q: What does the memory aid SnNout describe about a diagnostic test?
choices: A highly specific test, when positive, rules the disease in
A highly sensitive test, when negative, rules the disease out
A test with a high positive predictive value in any population
A test whose result does not depend on disease prevalence
quiz.why: SnNout pairs high sensitivity with a negative result to rule out, because a sensitive test produces few false negatives. Ruling in with a positive result from a specific test is SpPin, and predictive values always depend on prevalence, which is precisely what sensitivity and specificity do not.

quiz.q: The same test is used in an emergency department where 20 percent of tested patients have the disease and in a screening clinic where 1 percent do. What changes between the two settings?
choices: Sensitivity falls in the screening clinic
Specificity rises in the screening clinic
Positive predictive value falls in the screening clinic, so a larger share of positives are false
Nothing changes, because test characteristics are fixed properties
quiz.why: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself and do not move with the population. Predictive values do depend on prevalence, so in a low-prevalence setting a positive result is far more likely to be false, which is exactly why screening low-risk populations generates so much unnecessary follow-up testing.

quiz.q: A septic patient with pneumonia has a troponin of 0.09 ng/mL with an upper limit of 0.03, and no chest pain. What is the most accurate statement?
choices: This confirms an acute myocardial infarction and requires immediate catheterization
The result must be a laboratory error, since he has no chest pain
Troponin is specific to coronary plaque rupture, so a coronary cause is certain
Troponin indicates heart muscle injury, which occurs in sepsis, embolism, kidney failure, and heart failure as well as infarction
quiz.why: An elevated troponin means myocardial cells released protein, not that a coronary artery occluded; sepsis, pulmonary embolism, kidney failure, heart failure, myocarditis, and prolonged tachycardia all raise it. Calling it an error ignores a real finding that carries prognostic weight, and treating it as proof of infarction sends a septic patient to the wrong pathway.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old with two cardiac risk factors has a moderately suspicious history, non-specific ECG changes, and a normal troponin. What is his HEART score and the expected pathway?
choices: Score 4, moderate risk, observation with repeat troponins
Score 2, low risk, discharge with no follow-up needed
Score 8, high risk, admission to cardiology
Score 6, high risk, catheterization laboratory tonight
quiz.why: History 1, ECG 1, age 62 for 1, one to two risk factors for 1, and a normal troponin for 0 totals 4, which lands in the moderate band of 4 to 6 and means observation with serial troponins rather than discharge. High risk begins at 7, and even a genuinely low-risk patient still gets follow-up arranged.

quiz.q: A 38-year-old has pleuritic chest pain. The clinician's pretest probability for pulmonary embolism is roughly 10 percent, and all eight PERC criteria are negative. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Order a CT pulmonary angiogram regardless of the PERC result
No further testing for embolism is needed, because PERC applies at this pretest probability
Order a D-dimer to confirm the PERC result before stopping
Admit for serial D-dimers over the next 24 hours
quiz.why: PERC exists for exactly this situation: a pretest probability under about 15 percent with all eight criteria negative, where further testing causes more harm than it prevents. Adding a D-dimer here generates false positives that pull the patient into a contrast CT, and imaging or admission is more aggressive still.

quiz.q: Which patient can have the cervical spine cleared by NEXUS without any imaging?
choices: An alert, sober patient with no midline neck tenderness, no deficit, and an obviously fractured femur
A patient who smells strongly of alcohol but reports no neck pain
An alert, sober patient with no midline tenderness, no focal deficit, and no painful distracting injury
A confused elderly patient with no neck tenderness on palpation
quiz.why: All five NEXUS criteria must be satisfied simultaneously. A femur fracture is a painful distracting injury, intoxication invalidates the reliability of the exam, and confusion fails the normal alertness criterion, so each of those patients needs imaging or a different rule.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with pneumonia is confused, has a respiratory rate of 32, a blood pressure of 104/68, and a blood urea nitrogen of 24 mg/dL. What is the CURB-65 score and what does it imply?
choices: Score 1, outpatient treatment is appropriate
Score 2, discharge with a same-day recheck
Score 5, immediate comfort-focused care only
Score 4, admit and consider intensive care
quiz.why: Confusion, urea over 19, respiratory rate 30 or more, and age 65 or older each score one, for a total of 4, while the blood pressure does not qualify because the systolic is above 90 and the diastolic is above 60, the two ways that criterion can be met. Scores of 3 or more mean admission with intensive care considered, and the maximum possible score here would be 5.

quiz.q: A chart entry reads in full: Assessment, chest pain. Plan, admit. What is its principal deficiency?
choices: It documents no medical decision making, since it shows no problems considered, no data reviewed, and no risk assessment
It is too brief to be billable, which is the primary problem with it
It uses OPQRST where OLDCARTS would have been correct
It omits the patient's family history and immunization status
quiz.why: The medical decision making section exists to show which dangerous diagnoses were considered, what data was reviewed and why, and what level of risk justified the disposition. Billing follows from that documentation rather than being its purpose, and neither a different mnemonic nor a family history line would repair an assessment containing no reasoning.

quiz.q: A head CT report concludes: no acute intracranial abnormality, clinical correlation recommended. What does this tell the treating clinician?
choices: The brain is entirely normal and no further concern is warranted
Nothing urgent is visible on this study, and the clinical decision still rests with the treating clinician
The radiologist believes the patient is having a stroke
A repeat CT has been formally ordered for 6 hours from now
quiz.why: No acute abnormality means nothing urgent was seen on this particular study, which is narrower than a normal brain, and early ischemic stroke is frequently invisible on an initial non-contrast CT. Clinical correlation recommended hands the decision back to the person who holds the history, and it is not itself an order for repeat imaging.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure has drifted down over three checks and you want the provider at the bedside now. Which SBAR element is most often omitted, and what fixes it?
choices: Background is omitted, and reciting the full past medical history fixes it
Situation is omitted, and stating the room number fixes it
The recommendation is omitted, and saying I'm worried because, followed by what you want, fixes it
Assessment is omitted, and waiting for one more set of vitals fixes it
quiz.why: Most failed escalations are reports delivered without a request, so the missing piece is the recommendation. Naming your concern and what triggered it is the protected language that makes a concern actionable, whereas a full history buries the point and waiting for another set of vitals is precisely the delay escalation exists to prevent.

quiz.q: A man with chest pain and an abnormal ECG wants to leave. He is alert, explains his diagnosis back to you, states that he could die tonight, weighs that against needing to get home to his children, and gives the same answer each time you ask. What is the correct approach?
choices: He lacks capacity because the choice is unwise, so he may be held until he agrees
Have him sign the against-medical-advice form, which is sufficient legal protection by itself
Call security, since refusing cardiac care makes a patient a danger to himself
He has capacity: document the assessment and the specific risks discussed, offer what he will accept, and give prescriptions, follow-up, and return precautions
quiz.why: He demonstrates all four components of capacity, and a choice made with capacity remains his even when it is unwise. The signature by itself protects nothing; the documented capacity assessment and the specific risks explained are what matter, and detaining a patient who has capacity is false imprisonment rather than safe practice.

scenarios.title: Chest pain, from the doorway to the disposition
scenarios.intro:
This is a reasoning walkthrough, not a procedure. There is no equipment to reach for and no protocol to follow, only the thinking, one decision at a time.

A 58-year-old man has been roomed for chest pain. The triage note reads: **anxiety, history of panic attacks.** Work the case the way a clinician would, and notice at each step which choice is reasoning and which is a shortcut.

steps.prompt:
You stop in the doorway before you say anything. He is sitting upright on the edge of the stretcher, shirt off, a sheen of sweat across his forehead, one hand held flat against his breastbone. He answers you in full sentences. The room is not warm.

What do you do with the triage label?

choices.text: Accept the triage impression, plan for a quiet room and reassurance.
choices.feedback: This is anchoring and diagnosis momentum in a single move. A triage label is a hypothesis written in 15 seconds by someone with less information than you have right now. Sweating at rest in a cool room with a flat palm on the sternum is a cardiac pattern until something proves otherwise.

choices.text: Register sick from the doorway, the sweating, the posture, the flat hand on the chest, and treat the triage label as unproven.
choices.feedback: Correct. The doorway impression is real data. Sweating at rest is a sympathetic surge, and a flat palm pressed on the sternum describes pressure rather than a point of pain, which is how patients show you a cardiac quality without having the word for it.

choices.text: Form no impression at all until the vital signs and an ECG are available.
choices.feedback: Not harmful, but you are throwing away free information. His vitals here are close to unremarkable, a rate of 92 and a pressure of 156/94 would stop nobody, and if you wait for numbers to tell you a patient is sick you will be late on every patient who compensates well.

steps.prompt:
You take the story. Three hours of pressure, like something sitting on me, under the breastbone, which began while he carried groceries up a flight of stairs. `6/10`. It comes with nausea and sweating and eases a little at rest. Pressing on his chest does not reproduce it. He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol, smokes a pack a day and has for 30 years, and his father had a heart attack at 52.

Which additional questions are doing the most work right now?

choices.text: Ask how his mood has been, whether he is under stress, and whether he has had panic attacks before.
choices.feedback: These questions only hunt for evidence supporting the label you were handed. Even if every answer is yes, an anxious man can have a heart attack, and searching for confirmation of the benign answer is exactly how premature closure happens.

choices.text: Ask whether the pain tore or ripped through to his back, whether he has had recent surgery, a long flight, or leg swelling, and whether he has had fever or a cough.
choices.feedback: Right. These are the pertinent negatives for the killers: dissection, pulmonary embolism, and pneumonia. Asked because of a differential and recorded whether present or absent, they are what makes a note show reasoning instead of just findings.

choices.text: Run a complete head-to-toe review of systems before doing anything else.
choices.feedback: Thorough but misaimed for this encounter. A focused review of the two to four systems touching your differential buys the same safety in a fraction of the time. The full review of systems belongs in the admission history and physical, where that team owns the whole patient.

steps.prompt: Someone asks what you think. Say your differential out loud, the way it would be said on rounds.

choices.text: Chest pain, probably cardiac.
choices.feedback: Not wrong, just not useful. It names no alternatives and gives no reasons, so nobody can check your thinking or catch what you left out. A differential that cannot be audited is not doing its job.

choices.text: Acute coronary syndrome first, because of the exertional pressure, the sweating, three risk factors and the family history. Pulmonary embolism is possible but there is no low oxygen, no leg findings, no immobilization. Dissection is least likely, but I want pressures in both arms. Pneumonia does not fit, no fever and no cough.
choices.feedback: That is the three-item habit with an honest outlier: named diagnoses, one reason each, and a specific thing you want checked. It is short enough to say in a hallway and complete enough for someone to act on.

choices.text: It could be anything from reflux to a heart attack to a clot to costochondritis to shingles to a panic attack.
choices.feedback: A list of twenty is the same as no list. Nothing is ranked, nothing is excluded, and nobody can act on it. The entire point of ordering a differential is that the order decides what happens next.

steps.prompt: The ECG shows sinus rhythm with `1 mm` of ST depression in V4 through V6. The first troponin is `0.04 ng/mL` against an upper limit of `0.03`. Arm pressures are within `4 mmHg` of each other. Someone suggests adding a D-dimer, just to be safe.

choices.text: Send it. More information is always safer.
choices.feedback: This is the order-everything reflex. His pretest probability for embolism is low, D-dimer is only 40 to 50 percent specific, and a false positive commits him to a contrast CT with radiation for a disease the history already argued against, while the real pathway waits.

choices.text: No. His pretest probability for embolism is low and the result would not change the plan either way, because the ECG and troponin have already set the pathway.
choices.feedback: Correct, and for the correct reason. Order a test when you already know what each possible result would change. Here a positive and a negative both lead to the same next steps, which is the definition of a test that should not be sent.

choices.text: No, because a negative D-dimer can never rule out a pulmonary embolism in anyone.
choices.feedback: Right conclusion, wrong reason, and the wrong reason will hurt you later. A negative D-dimer does exclude embolism in a genuinely low-risk patient, which is precisely what the test is for. The reason to skip it here is that the result changes nothing.

steps.prompt:
Score him. History is highly suspicious for `2`, the ECG shows significant ST deviation for `2`, age 58 gives `1`, three or more risk factors gives `2`, and a troponin between one and three times normal gives `1`. Total HEART score `8`.

What does that mean, and what happens next?

choices.text: High risk. He is admitted with cardiology involved, on continuous monitoring, with a repeat troponin and ECG at 3 hours, to a telemetry bed.
choices.feedback: Correct, and specific. A HEART score of 7 to 10 is the high band, and the disposition names a destination, a service, and a timeline, which is what makes it actually happen in a busy department.

choices.text: High risk, so he needs admission, though the service and the timing can be sorted out later.
choices.feedback: The risk read and the bucket are both right. What is missing is the specific ask. A disposition without a named destination, a named service, and a timeline stalls, and the patient stays in the hallway while everyone assumes someone else is arranging it.

choices.text: Moderate risk, so observe him for six hours and reassess.
choices.feedback: A HEART score of 8 sits in the high band of 7 to 10, which carries a major adverse cardiac event rate in the tens of percent. Observation with serial troponins is the moderate-risk pathway for scores of 4 to 6.

choices.text: Low risk with outpatient follow-up, since his vital signs are normal and he is comfortable at rest.
choices.feedback: Normal vital signs do not lower a HEART score, and comfort at rest is not reassurance in acute coronary syndrome, where the pain often eases between events. Low risk is a score of 0 to 3.

steps.prompt: Before the handoff you take a diagnostic time-out. What belongs in those twenty seconds, and in the sentence you hand over?

choices.text: Working diagnosis, what does not fit, the worst thing it could still be, then a handoff that opens with the one-liner and closes with what you want.
choices.feedback: Correct. The time-out is three questions and it takes less time than finding a pen. The handoff that opens with the one-liner and ends with a request is the one that gets acted on rather than filed.

choices.text: A summary of everything in the chart, in the order it was entered.
choices.feedback: Complete but unusable. The receiving clinician is assembling a picture and needs the one-liner first, the pertinent findings next, and the ask last. Chronological chart dumps bury the two sentences that matter.

choices.text: Nothing. The chart has it all and the next clinician can read it.
choices.feedback: The chart is a record, not a handoff. A large share of serious errors traced back to communication happen exactly here, in the gap between two people who each assumed the other had read it.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: the doorway impression comes first and it is data; the triage label is a hypothesis someone else wrote, not a finding; pertinent negatives are how you show which killers you considered; a test you would not act on differently should not be sent; and a disposition is only real when it names a destination, a service, and a timeline.

Notice what never happened in this case. Nobody ordered a test to feel safer, and nobody named the likely diagnosis before the dangerous ones had been addressed. That order, killers first and likely second, is the whole method.

scenarios.title: Writing the note on a case you just saw
scenarios.intro:
You saw the patient. Now write it up. At each step you are shown three versions of one section of the note, and you pick the best.

**The case:** a 24-year-old woman with 6 hours of abdominal pain that began around her navel and settled in the right lower quadrant, with nausea, one episode of vomiting, and no appetite. Last menstrual period 5 weeks ago, no vaginal bleeding or discharge, no burning with urination, no diarrhea.

**What you found:** `T 38.1 C, HR 104, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air`. Tender in the right lower quadrant with guarding, and pressing on the left lower quadrant reproduces pain on the right. Urine pregnancy test negative. Urinalysis with a few white cells, no nitrites, no blood.

choices.text: 24-year-old woman with abdominal pain. Rule out appendicitis.
choices.feedback: That is a hypothesis, not a subjective section. The chief complaint belongs in the patient's words with a duration, and the history of present illness has to contain a story that somebody else could reason from independently.

choices.text: 24-year-old woman with 6 hours of pain that began around the navel and moved to the right lower quadrant, with nausea, one episode of vomiting, and loss of appetite. Last menstrual period 5 weeks ago. Denies vaginal bleeding or discharge, burning with urination, or diarrhea.
choices.feedback: Correct. It is chronological, it preserves the migration of the pain that carries most of the diagnostic weight, and the denials are the pertinent negatives that show you considered ectopic pregnancy, urinary infection, and gastroenteritis.

choices.text: Patient complains of severe abdominal pain, appears uncomfortable, abdomen tender to palpation in the right lower quadrant with guarding.
choices.feedback: Everything after the first clause is objective. What you observed and measured belongs in O, and mixing the two makes the note hard to read and hard to defend, because no reader can separate what she reported from what you found.

choices.text: Vitals stable. Abdomen tender in the right lower quadrant, consistent with appendicitis.
choices.feedback: Two problems. Vitals stable is not a measurement, and it hides a temperature of 38.1 with a heart rate of 104. And consistent with appendicitis is an interpretation, which belongs in the assessment where a reader can weigh it.

choices.text: T 38.1 C, HR 104, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air. Alert, uncomfortable. Abdomen soft elsewhere, tender in the right lower quadrant with voluntary guarding, pain in the right lower quadrant on palpation of the left. Urine pregnancy negative. Urinalysis with a few white cells, no nitrites, no blood.
choices.feedback: Correct. Every number is written out, the exam findings are described rather than labeled, and the results are stated without a verdict attached. A later reader can reach their own conclusion from this section, which is the test of a good O.

choices.text: T 38.1 C, HR 104, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air. Pregnancy test negative.
choices.feedback: Accurate as far as it goes, but the exam is missing entirely, and the exam is where the diagnosis lives in this case. Guarding and referred tenderness are the findings that separate appendicitis from a viral illness.

choices.text: Abdominal pain.
choices.feedback: Restating the complaint is not an assessment. It shows no thinking, and in a later chart review it reads exactly as though none happened.

choices.text: Appendicitis.
choices.feedback: A working diagnosis with no reasoning and no alternatives. If she turns out to have ovarian torsion, nothing in this note shows that anyone ever considered one, which is a problem for her care first and for the chart second.

choices.text: 24-year-old woman with 6 hours of migratory right lower quadrant pain, fever to 38.1, focal tenderness with guarding and referred tenderness. Most consistent with acute appendicitis. Ovarian torsion and tubo-ovarian abscess remain on the differential and are the reason for pelvic imaging. Ectopic pregnancy excluded by a negative pregnancy test. Urinary infection unlikely without nitrites or urinary symptoms.
choices.feedback: Correct. A one-liner, a working diagnosis, the live alternatives with what is being done about them, and the excluded ones with the evidence that excluded them. This paragraph is the medical decision making.

choices.text: CT abdomen and pelvis. Surgery consult.
choices.feedback: The right two items with none of the surrounding care. Nothing here addresses pain, fluids, whether she may eat or drink, antibiotics, or reassessment, and a plan that lists only tests leaves the patient waiting untreated.

choices.text: IV access, nothing by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, CT abdomen and pelvis with pelvic ultrasound to evaluate for torsion, surgery consulted, antibiotics per surgery, reassess after imaging. Disposition anticipated as admission.
choices.feedback: Correct. It covers what happens to the patient as well as what gets ordered, names the second study and the reason for it, and states the anticipated disposition so that everyone downstream is working toward the same endpoint.

choices.text: Pain medicine and discharge with instructions to follow up with her own doctor.
choices.feedback: Unsafe. A febrile patient with focal tenderness and guarding has a possible surgical abdomen, and sending her home without imaging or a surgical opinion risks perforation. Follow up with your doctor is not a plan for someone who may need an operation today.

steps.prompt: Later that shift a different patient, a 30-year-old man whose abdominal pain resolved and whose workup was unremarkable, is going home. Choose his **return precautions**.

choices.text: Return if symptoms worsen.
choices.feedback: Boilerplate. It names no trigger the patient can recognize, so it neither protects him nor demonstrates anything about your thinking. Worsen means nothing at two in the morning to someone deciding whether to come back.

choices.text: Come back right away if the pain returns and stays in one spot, if it becomes severe, if you develop a fever over 100.4 F, if you vomit repeatedly or cannot keep fluids down, or if the pain moves to the lower right side. See your doctor in 2 days if you are not fully better.
choices.feedback: Correct. Specific, recognizable triggers in plain language with a timeframe and a follow-up. These are the safety net for the diagnoses the workup could not exclude, which is exactly what return precautions exist to cover.

choices.text: No return precautions needed, since the workup was negative and he feels better.
choices.feedback: A negative workup means nothing dangerous was found in the hours he was here, not that nothing will develop. Early appendicitis frequently looks unremarkable at hour four and obvious at hour twelve, and the return precaution is the only thing bridging that gap.

scenarios.debrief:
The shape of a good note is the shape of good thinking. Subjective holds the story, Objective holds what you measured with no verdicts attached, Assessment holds the reasoning including the alternatives and what excluded them, and Plan covers the patient and not just the orders.

Two sections carry disproportionate weight. The assessment paragraph is the medical decision making, and it is what a reader years later uses to judge whether the care was reasonable. The return precautions are the safety net for everything the workup could not exclude, and they have to name triggers a frightened person can actually recognize at home.
